newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Srebrenica killer felt "worthless" after massacre.
newsitem.headline: Srebrenica killer felt "worthless" after massacre.

text.p: A Bosnian Croat who took part in a massacre of Moslems from Srebrenica said on Tuesday the killing had made him feel worthless, but he would have faced certain death himself if he had defied orders to open fire.
"I'm sure I would have been killed myself if I had not obeyed the order," 24-year-old Drazen Erdemovic told the Hague-based United Nations war crimes tribunal.
"It destroyed me. It killed me. I simply felt my life was worthless after that," he said through an interpreter.
U.N. war crimes prosecutors allege that Bosnian Serb forces summarily executed thousands of Moslem men after seizing the U.N. protected "safe area" of Srebrenica in July 1995.
Erdemovic pleaded guilty in May to taking part in the wholesale slaughter of hundreds of unarmed Moslem men after the eastern Bosnian town fell to the Serbs.
He told prosecutors that Moslems were taken in buses to a farm at Pilica near the town of Zvornik where they were shot dead by his unit of the Bosnian Serb Army.
Erdemovic said he had refused to take part in another massacre of Moslems at Pilica and had later been shot in the stomach and lungs by a member of his unit for insubordination.
At this point he stood up and raised his shirt to display his scars to the panel of three U.N. judges.
After being discharged from a military hospital in Belgrade, Erdemovic said he had sent his Serb wife and their young son to his in-laws in Tuzla then told his story to U.S.television network ABC.
He was arrested by the Serbian authorities in March 1996 and sent to The Hague at the end of that month.
Erdemovic said he had decided to speak out about the killings to reveal the truth about Srebrenica.
"I just want the truth to be known and for someone to understand that this actually happened, how these people lost their lives," he said.
"I didn't want to fight a war. I lost friends of various nationalities. All because that Mafia led us ordinary people into a war. That is why I'm testifying here today," he said.
Prosecutors argued earlier on Tuesday that Erdemovic should be given a lenient sentence because he had provided valuable information about the killings after the fall of Srebrenica.
Prosecutor Eric Ostberg of Sweden told the tribunal Erdemovic had cooperated fully with the U.N. investigation into the massacre and had been the main source of information about killings at Pilica.

"His role in the mass execution of innocent civilians at Pilica was significant. However, it is the view of the prosecutor that...his sentence should be substantially mitigated," documents submitted by the prosecution said.
Ostberg and U.S. prosecutor Mark Harmon said Erdemovic deserved to be treated leniently because he had been forced to commit the crime by his superiors.
Furthermore, he had voluntarily surrendered himself to the tribunal, confessed his guilt and consistently shown remorse for his role in the killings.
His sentence is expected early next month and will be the first handed down by the tribunal, which cannot impose the death penalty. Its maximum sentence is life imprisonment.
The tribunal has already charged deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic with genocide over the Srebrenica massacre.
Both men remain at large, in common with the majority of the 75 suspects indicted by the tribunal.
